items.prompt: Marco spent the same total 20 hours as Sofia, split evenly across six topics instead of concentrated on the two that mattered most. What does his outcome mainly show about depth?
choices: That going deep on a larger number of topics is always the objectively safer approach
That an hour spent going deep on one topic is an hour unavailable for another — depth is never free just because time was available
That splitting time evenly is essentially risk-free since nothing gets fully ignored
That Marco simply had notably worse luck on the day of the actual test than Sofia did
items.explanation: Depth costs real hours drawn from one shared pool. Marco's even split didn't protect him from a bad outcome — it guaranteed his highest-stakes topics got no more attention than his lowest-stakes one, because every hour given to a low-value topic was an hour taken from a high-value one.
items.reference:
The claim: Depth is expensive — every hour spent going deep on one thing is unavailable for another.

Why: An even split doesn't reduce this cost, it just spends it uniformly regardless of which topics actually deserve it.

items.prompt: "It doesn't hurt to go a little deeper on this, I have the time" — what's the flaw in that reasoning, according to this unit?
choices: There's no real flaw here — any extra depth is always a pure bonus if the time genuinely exists
It ignores that the time being spent is drawn from the same limited budget every other topic is competing for
Going deeper on any given topic always improves overall preparedness by the exact same fixed amount
Depth only ever carries a real cost when the total time available happens to be small
items.explanation: "I have the time" treats the hour as free-floating, but it's still coming out of a fixed total budget — spending it here means it can't be spent on whichever topic would have used it better. The cost exists regardless of how much total time is available.
items.reference:
The claim: Depth is expensive — every hour spent going deep on one thing is unavailable for another.

Why: An even split doesn't reduce this cost, it just spends it uniformly regardless of which topics actually deserve it.

items.prompt: Why does this unit treat 'going a little deeper on everything' as the riskier strategy, not the safer one?
choices: Because it ends up taking more total time overall than any properly triaged approach would
Because it spends the same fixed hours on every topic regardless of how much any one of them actually matters, so high-stakes topics get no extra protection
Because most people find spreading effort evenly more mentally exhausting than triaging
Because it's simply impossible to finish an even split across every topic before a deadline
items.explanation: The risk isn't the total time spent — it's that an even split can't respond to which topics actually matter more. High-stakes and low-stakes topics get identical treatment, which is exactly backwards from what a good allocation would do.
items.reference:
The claim: Depth is expensive — every hour spent going deep on one thing is unavailable for another.

Why: An even split doesn't reduce this cost, it just spends it uniformly regardless of which topics actually deserve it.

items.prompt: Marco and Sofia spent the exact same 20 total hours preparing. What actually explains why Sofia's preparation held up better?
choices: Sofia was simply a faster, more naturally talented learner overall than Marco was
Sofia decided in advance which of those hours mattered most, rather than spreading them evenly
Sofia happened to have access to noticeably better study material than Marco did
Sofia actually spent more total hours preparing overall than Marco ultimately did
items.explanation: The total time was identical. The difference was entirely in how it was allocated — Sofia decided ahead of time which topics deserved the bulk of her hours, while Marco split his time without making that call at all.
items.reference:
The claim: Same total hours, very different outcomes.

Why: The gap was entirely in how the hours were allocated, not in how many hours existed.

items.prompt: If Marco had simply been given 30 hours instead of 20, but still split them evenly across all six topics, what would this unit predict?
choices: He would now clearly outperform Sofia, since having more total time always wins out
His highest-stakes topics would still get no more attention than his lowest-stakes ones — the allocation problem, not the total amount, is what mattered
The extra hours would automatically get redirected toward his single weakest topic
There would be essentially no meaningful difference at all from the original 20-hour case
items.explanation: More total hours doesn't fix an allocation problem — it just gives the same flawed allocation strategy more hours to spread evenly and just as thinly across topics that don't equally deserve it. The visa paperwork and bank account would still get the same proportion of attention as tipping customs.
items.reference:
The claim: Same total hours, very different outcomes.

Why: The gap was entirely in how the hours were allocated, not in how many hours existed.

items.prompt: What is the single biggest difference between how Marco and Sofia approached their 20 hours?
choices: Sofia made a deliberate decision about which topics deserved the most time; Marco didn't make that decision at all
Sofia simply studied for a greater number of total hours than Marco managed to
Marco made use of noticeably better study techniques on each individual topic
Sofia happened to have prior experience with some of the topics going in
items.explanation: The whole scenario holds total hours, the topic list, and the starting knowledge roughly equal on purpose, to isolate one variable: whether a deliberate allocation decision was made at all, versus time being split by default.
items.reference:
The claim: Same total hours, very different outcomes.

Why: The gap was entirely in how the hours were allocated, not in how many hours existed.

items.prompt: What does "just-in-time learning" mean, as this unit uses the term?
choices: Cramming in as much total material as possible right before an approaching deadline
Deliberately staying shallow on something now, trusting you can learn it well enough exactly when the real need shows up
Going fully deep on a topic the very instant you first hear it mentioned
Studying a topic in short, spaced-out sessions instead of one single long one
items.explanation: Just-in-time learning is a deliberate choice to stay shallow now on the trust that the real skill of picking it up quickly, when the need is genuine, will be enough — not procrastination and not a study-scheduling technique.
items.reference:
The claim: Just-in-time learning means staying shallow on purpose, trusting a fast catch-up when the need is real.

Why: It's safe exactly when the cost of learning something later is low.

items.prompt: Sofia only skimmed the public transit system before her move, planning to figure it out properly once she arrived. What kind of learning strategy is that?
choices: Just-in-case learning
Just-in-time learning
Avoidance — she simply chose not to learn it
Spaced repetition
items.explanation: Deliberately deferring the real depth until the need is concrete — she'll figure it out once she's actually navigating the city — is the definition of just-in-time learning, not avoidance, since the plan to learn it later is intentional.
items.reference:
The claim: Just-in-time learning means staying shallow on purpose, trusting a fast catch-up when the need is real.

Why: It's safe exactly when the cost of learning something later is low.

items.prompt: What does "just-in-case learning" mean, as this unit uses the term?
choices: Learning something now because it might matter later, before there's a concrete need for it
Learning something only once you've already confirmed for certain you'll need it
A spaced-repetition study technique that reviews material at increasing intervals
Learning a given topic exclusively by relying on a single trusted source
items.explanation: Just-in-case learning means investing depth now on a hunch it might be useful later, rather than because a concrete need already exists — the opposite posture from just-in-time learning.
items.reference:
The claim: Just-in-case learning is often wasted, but pays off for genuinely foundational material.

Why: Most 'might need this' material never gets used — the exception is material that accelerates many other things.

items.prompt: According to this unit, is just-in-case learning generally a good use of study time?
choices: Yes, always — it's generally better to be over-prepared than it is to be under-prepared
Usually not — most 'might need this' material never actually gets used, though it can pay off for foundational material
No, never — it should always be avoided entirely in favor of just-in-time learning instead
It depends purely on how much free time happens to be available, and nothing else
items.explanation: Just-in-case learning is usually wasted effort, since most hedged-on material never gets used. The genuine exception is foundational material — something that accelerates learning many other things, which changes the calculus even without certainty it will matter on its own.
items.reference:
The claim: Just-in-case learning is often wasted, but pays off for genuinely foundational material.

Why: Most 'might need this' material never gets used — the exception is material that accelerates many other things.

items.prompt: This unit's triage heuristic weighs three factors about a topic to decide whether it deserves deep study. Which three?
choices: How interesting it is, how long it takes to explain, and how many sources exist on it
How likely it is to matter, how costly it would be to learn later, and how foundational it is
How difficult it is, how popular it is, and how recently it was published
How much time is left before the deadline, how tired you are, and how motivated you feel
items.explanation: The three factors are: likelihood the topic will actually matter, the cost of learning it later if skipped now, and whether it's foundational enough to accelerate learning other things — not difficulty, popularity, or personal energy level.
items.reference:
The claim: Three factors decide whether a topic deserves deep study: likelihood, cost-to-learn-later, foundational-ness.

Why: Together they separate 'deep now' from 'just-in-time' from 'skip.'

items.prompt: "Cost to learn later" in this unit's triage heuristic refers to what, specifically?
choices: How much actual money a course or resource covering the topic happens to cost
How expensive — in time, difficulty, or missed windows — it would be to pick the topic up when the need actually arrives
How emotionally uncomfortable or tedious the topic itself is to sit down and study
How many other people in the group already happen to know the topic well
items.explanation: Cost to learn later is about the practical difficulty of catching up when the real need shows up — including narrow windows (a filing deadline) and topics that get genuinely harder to learn after the fact — not money, emotional discomfort, or how common the knowledge already is.
items.reference:
The claim: Three factors decide whether a topic deserves deep study: likelihood, cost-to-learn-later, foundational-ness.

Why: Together they separate 'deep now' from 'just-in-time' from 'skip.'

items.prompt: A topic scores low on "likely to matter" but the heuristic still recommends deep study now. What's the most likely reason?
choices: The topic simply happened to be the very first one listed near the top
It scored high on foundational-ness — it accelerates learning many other things, even without certainty it will matter on its own
It happened to be the single easiest topic on the whole list to study
The person studying it simply happens to personally enjoy that topic more
items.explanation: Foundational-ness is the one factor that can push a topic toward deep study even when likelihood is low, because its value comes from accelerating everything downstream of it, not from mattering on its own.
items.reference:
The claim: Three factors decide whether a topic deserves deep study: likelihood, cost-to-learn-later, foundational-ness.

Why: Together they separate 'deep now' from 'just-in-time' from 'skip.'

items.prompt: This unit's core 2x2 table crosses two questions about a topic. Which two?
choices: How likely it is to matter, and how costly it would be to learn later
How long it takes to learn, and how many people already know it
How interesting it is, and how recently it was introduced
How foundational it is, and how popular it is
items.explanation: The core table crosses likelihood-to-matter against cost-to-learn-later, producing four zones: deep now, just-in-time, skip, and cheap-insurance skim. Foundational-ness is a third factor layered on top, not one of the two table axes.
items.reference:
The claim: Crossing likelihood-to-matter with cost-to-learn-later produces four zones.

Why: Deep-now is reserved for topics that are both likely to matter and costly to learn late.

items.prompt: A topic is likely to matter, and cheap to learn later if skipped now. Which zone of the 2x2 table does it fall into?
choices: Deep now — the zone reserved for topics that are both likely and costly later
Just-in-time — skim now, go deep only when the real need shows up
Skip entirely — the zone reserved for topics unlikely to matter and cheap later
Cheap insurance skim — reserved for low-likelihood but costly-later foundational items
items.explanation: Likely-to-matter plus cheap-to-learn-later is exactly the just-in-time zone: since catching up later is cheap, pre-loading depth now would be wasted effort relative to simply learning it well when the need is real.
items.reference:
The claim: Crossing likelihood-to-matter with cost-to-learn-later produces four zones.

Why: Deep-now is reserved for topics that are both likely to matter and costly to learn late.

items.prompt: Sofia's visa paperwork and bank account both landed in the "deep now" zone. What made them both land there?
choices: They were both likely to matter soon and costly to learn later if skipped
They were both interesting to her
They were both cheap to learn later, so she over-invested by mistake
They were both unlikely to matter but she studied them anyway out of caution
items.explanation: Deep now is the zone for topics that are both likely to matter soon and costly to get wrong or catch up on later — exactly the combination visa paperwork and banking had, which is why they got the bulk of her 20 hours.
items.reference:
The claim: Crossing likelihood-to-matter with cost-to-learn-later produces four zones.

Why: Deep-now is reserved for topics that are both likely to matter and costly to learn late.

items.prompt: Which combination of the two axes puts a topic in the "deep now" zone?
choices: Unlikely to matter and cheap to learn later
Likely to matter and costly to learn later
Unlikely to matter and costly to learn later
Likely to matter and cheap to learn later
items.explanation: Deep now requires both a high likelihood of mattering and a high cost if you wait to learn it later — that combination is where pre-loading depth actually pays off, since waiting is both risky and expensive.
items.reference:
The claim: Deep-now sits at the intersection of high likelihood and high cost-to-learn-later.

Why: Both conditions are needed — either one alone points to a different zone.

items.prompt: A topic is highly likely to matter, but cheap to learn later. Is "deep now" still the right call for it?
choices: Yes — likelihood alone, on its own, is already enough to justify deep study right now
No — since it's cheap to learn later, just-in-time is the better fit even though it's likely to matter
Yes, but only if the topic also happens to be genuinely foundational as well
No, it should actually be skipped entirely, regardless of how likely it is to matter
items.explanation: Deep now needs both conditions, not just likelihood. If catching up later is cheap, the safer, cheaper play is just-in-time — skim now, invest the real depth only once the need is concrete.
items.reference:
The claim: Deep-now sits at the intersection of high likelihood and high cost-to-learn-later.

Why: Both conditions are needed — either one alone points to a different zone.

items.prompt: A topic is unlikely to matter, cheap to learn later if it somehow does, and not foundational. What does the model recommend?
choices: Deep study now, as a precaution
Skip it — not worth even a skim
Just-in-time learning
A cheap skim as insurance
items.explanation: When a topic is unlikely to matter, cheap to catch up on if it does, and doesn't unlock anything else, there's no factor left pointing toward spending any time on it at all — it's the one cell that's genuinely fine to skip entirely.
items.reference:
The claim: Low likelihood plus low cost-to-learn-later, with no foundational value, means skip entirely.

Why: Nothing about the topic points toward spending any of the limited budget on it.

items.prompt: Sofia skipped local slang almost entirely. Which combination of factors justified that?
choices: Unlikely to matter soon, cheap to pick up naturally, and not foundational
It was likely to matter soon, but was also cheap to learn later if needed
It was costly to learn later, but was also judged unlikely to matter at all
It was judged highly foundational, but also unlikely to matter on its own
items.explanation: Local slang scored low on likelihood (not urgent in month one), low on cost-to-learn-later (immersion picks it up naturally), and wasn't foundational to anything else on her list — the combination that makes skipping it entirely the right call.
items.reference:
The claim: Low likelihood plus low cost-to-learn-later, with no foundational value, means skip entirely.

Why: Nothing about the topic points toward spending any of the limited budget on it.

items.prompt: A topic is unlikely to matter and costly to learn later if it turns out you needed it. What's the one thing that could still push it toward deep study now, according to this unit?
choices: If it simply happens to be the topic the learner personally finds most interesting
If it's foundational — it accelerates learning many other things, whether or not it matters on its own
If a trusted friend happens to recommend studying that particular topic
If there's simply extra leftover time available with nothing else left to do
items.explanation: Foundational-ness is the specific override: a topic that unlocks or speeds up learning many other things can be worth deep study even without confidence it will matter on its own, because its value comes from what it accelerates downstream.
items.reference:
The claim: Foundational-ness can push a topic toward deep study even without certainty it will matter.

Why: Its value comes from accelerating other learning, not from mattering on its own — but it still competes for the same limited hours.

items.prompt: Someone argues a topic is foundational, so it deserves deep study time right now regardless of anything else going on. Is 'it's foundational' alone a sufficient justification?
choices: Yes — foundational-ness always automatically overrides every other consideration entirely
No — foundational-ness raises the topic's priority, but it still competes with everything else for the same limited hours
No — foundational-ness is actually irrelevant to the triage decision altogether
Yes, but only for topics that also happen to be relatively easy to learn
items.explanation: Foundational-ness is one input into the decision, not an automatic override. It makes a topic a stronger candidate than it would otherwise be, but it still has to be weighed against everything else competing for the same scarce time — including urgent, likely-to-matter items already on the list.
items.reference:
The claim: Foundational-ness can push a topic toward deep study even without certainty it will matter.

Why: Its value comes from accelerating other learning, not from mattering on its own — but it still competes for the same limited hours.

items.prompt: Why did Sofia give local language basics only 1.25 hours, even after judging it foundational?
choices: Because foundational topics, by this unit's own account, never deserve significant study time
Because the marginal benefit of more hours there didn't outweigh finishing her higher-priority visa and banking prep, given her limited total budget
Because she didn't actually, deep down, believe it was genuinely foundational at all
Because basic language skills were judged to have essentially no cost to learn later
items.explanation: Being foundational made language basics a stronger candidate than a purely non-foundational low-priority topic, but it still had to compete against visa paperwork and banking for the same 20 hours — and she judged those two had the higher claim on her limited time.
items.reference:
The claim: Foundational-ness can push a topic toward deep study even without certainty it will matter.

Why: Its value comes from accelerating other learning, not from mattering on its own — but it still competes for the same limited hours.

items.prompt: Marco treated every item on his list as equally worth studying, on the reasoning that any of them 'might come in handy.' What does this unit call that mistake?
choices: Correctly and appropriately applying just-in-time learning to every item on the list
Treating just-in-case learning as the default for everything, when it should be reserved for foundational material
Simply under-preparing relative to Sofia, with no particular named mistake behind it
Applying the two-axis test correctly overall, just running into some bad luck
items.explanation: Marco effectively hedged on every item — just-in-case learning applied uniformly — without asking whether any given item was actually likely to matter, costly to learn later, or foundational. Most 'might come in handy' material never gets used, which is exactly why that default is a trap.
items.reference:
The claim: Just-in-case learning is usually wasted, but pays off for genuinely foundational material.

Why: Most items that 'might matter' never get used — treating every item that way spends the whole budget on hedges.

items.prompt: Under what condition does just-in-case learning genuinely pay off, according to this unit?
choices: Whenever there's spare time available
When the topic is foundational — it accelerates learning many other things, not just itself
Whenever the topic feels important, regardless of the reasoning behind that feeling
Only when the person has already failed to learn it just-in-time once before
items.explanation: The genuine exception to 'just-in-case is usually wasted' is foundational material — topics whose value comes from speeding up everything downstream of them, which makes the investment worthwhile even without certainty the topic itself will matter.
items.reference:
The claim: Just-in-case learning is usually wasted, but pays off for genuinely foundational material.

Why: Most items that 'might matter' never get used — treating every item that way spends the whole budget on hedges.

items.prompt: Why is 'it might be useful' not, by itself, a good enough reason to go deep on a topic?
choices: Because almost anything could conceivably be useful, so the bar has to be higher than mere possibility
Because usefulness of any kind can never be reliably predicted in advance, under any circumstances
Because deep study of any topic is, according to this unit, always ultimately wasted effort
Because it's technically impossible to ever study a topic purely 'just in case' of future need
items.explanation: Almost anything clears the bar of 'might conceivably be useful' — that's exactly why it's a weak filter. The real questions are how likely it is to matter in practice, how costly skipping it would be, and whether it's foundational, not whether usefulness is merely conceivable.
items.reference:
The claim: Just-in-case learning is usually wasted, but pays off for genuinely foundational material.

Why: Most items that 'might matter' never get used — treating every item that way spends the whole budget on hedges.

items.prompt: Sofia scored health insurance enrollment as low-cost-to-learn-later, reasoning it would work like tipping customs. What actually went wrong?
choices: The triage method itself turned out to be fundamentally flawed and needs a fourth factor added
One input to the method — her estimate of cost-to-learn-later — was wrong, based on a false analogy rather than checking the actual rules
She simply ran out of available time to study the topic at all before the deadline
The topic actually wasn't on her original triage list to begin with
items.explanation: The three-question process was applied correctly; the answer to one of the questions was wrong. She assumed a low cost-to-learn-later by analogy to tipping customs, without checking whether the actual enrollment system had a hard deadline — which it did.
items.reference:
The claim: Sofia's process was sound; one input to it (an unchecked analogy) was wrong.

Why: A correct process can still produce a bad outcome when it's fed a bad estimate.

items.prompt: What specifically made the health insurance item different from tipping customs, even though Sofia initially scored them similarly?
choices: Health insurance had a hard 10-day enrollment window with real consequences for missing it; tipping customs had no deadline and low consequences either way
Health insurance simply turned out to be more interesting for her to research
Tipping customs, it later turned out, also carried a strict enrollment deadline
Nothing at all — the two items were genuinely equivalent, and she simply got unlucky
items.explanation: The two topics only looked similar on the surface (both felt like 'ask someone once you're there' topics). The actual cost-to-learn-later was very different: health insurance had a narrow, consequential deadline; tipping customs had none. Checking the real rules, rather than trusting the surface similarity, would have caught this.
items.reference:
The claim: Sofia's process was sound; one input to it (an unchecked analogy) was wrong.

Why: A correct process can still produce a bad outcome when it's fed a bad estimate.

items.prompt: What general lesson does the health insurance miss point to, beyond that one specific topic?
choices: That real deadlines can never actually be predicted in advance, so triage itself is pointless
For any item with real consequences attached, 'cost to learn later' deserves an actual check rather than being estimated purely by analogy to a different, lower-stakes item
That every single topic should always receive deep study time, purely to be safe
That just-in-time learning as a strategy should never be used for anything at all
items.explanation: The specific failure was estimating cost-to-learn-later by loose analogy instead of checking the real facts, for an item where being wrong had real consequences. The general lesson is to spend the few minutes verifying that estimate specifically when the stakes of being wrong are high — not to abandon triage altogether.
items.reference:
The claim: Sofia's process was sound; one input to it (an unchecked analogy) was wrong.

Why: A correct process can still produce a bad outcome when it's fed a bad estimate.

items.prompt: Sofia's triage process led to one correct call (visa/banking) and one costly miss (health insurance). What does having both outcomes in the same scenario demonstrate?
choices: That the whole triage process is fundamentally unreliable and simply shouldn't be trusted
That prioritization is a bet made with incomplete information, not a guarantee of a good outcome every time
That she should have gone deep on absolutely every single topic instead, no exceptions
That the health insurance miss by itself proves the whole two-axis model is wrong
items.explanation: A well-reasoned triage process improves the odds of good outcomes, but it's still a bet made with whatever information is available at the time — it doesn't guarantee every individual call turns out right, which is exactly what this scenario is built to show.
items.reference:
The claim: A sound process can still produce a bad individual outcome — that doesn't make the process bad.

Why: Judge the process by the quality of its reasoning given available information, not by any single result.

items.prompt: Someone concludes that because the health insurance triage went wrong, Sofia's whole triage approach must be a bad one. What's the flaw in that reasoning?
choices: There's no real flaw at all — one bad outcome is already sufficient proof the whole approach is bad
It judges the process purely by one outcome, rather than by the quality of reasoning applied given what was actually knowable at the time
The visa and banking successes simply don't count as meaningful evidence of anything
Triage decisions of this kind can never actually be meaningfully evaluated at all
items.explanation: A single bad outcome doesn't retroactively prove a process was flawed, any more than a single good outcome proves it was flawless — the process should be judged by whether the reasoning was sound given the information available, separate from how any individual bet happened to land.
items.reference:
The claim: A sound process can still produce a bad individual outcome — that doesn't make the process bad.

Why: Judge the process by the quality of its reasoning given available information, not by any single result.

items.prompt: What's the key difference between calling a decision process 'bad' and calling an individual outcome 'bad'?
choices: There is no real meaningful difference at all between evaluating a process and an outcome
A process is evaluated by the quality of reasoning given available information; an outcome is what actually happened, which can go wrong even from sound reasoning
An individual outcome is always a fully reliable signal of the underlying process quality
Process quality can only ever be judged once every single possible outcome is already known
items.explanation: A process can be well-reasoned and still produce a bad outcome, because outcomes depend on information that wasn't available at decision time (like the exact enrollment deadline). Separating 'was this reasoned well' from 'did it turn out well' is what lets someone learn the right lesson from a miss instead of the wrong one.
items.reference:
The claim: A sound process can still produce a bad individual outcome — that doesn't make the process bad.

Why: Judge the process by the quality of its reasoning given available information, not by any single result.

items.prompt: By week two, Sofia learned her employer needed a local tax form filed within her first month — much sooner than she'd originally assumed. What did she do with that new information?
choices: Nothing at all — the original triage decision stands firm regardless of any new information
She revisited the triage decision on that item, moving it from 'skip' to 'deep now' based on the updated information
She concluded her entire original triage had been a total mistake and redid it from scratch
She simply ignored it, since tax filing hadn't appeared anywhere on her original list
items.explanation: Triage isn't a one-time, fixed decision — it's worth revisiting specific items once real information replaces the original guesses. She updated just the tax-filing item based on new, more accurate information about its actual deadline, without treating the whole original triage as invalid.
items.reference:
The claim: Triage should be revisited once real information replaces the original guesses, not fixed forever after the first pass.

Why: A changed input justifies an updated decision without implying the earlier decision was wrong given what was known then.

items.prompt: Local tax filing moved from 'skip entirely' to 'deep now' after Sofia learned the real deadline. Does this mean her original day-one decision to skip it was a mistake?
choices: Yes — by this unit's reasoning, she really should have caught this already back on day one
No — 'not due for months' was a reasonable basis for skipping it given what she knew on day one; the correction came from new information, not a flaw in the original reasoning
Yes, because any later correction to a plan always means the original call was simply wrong
The question is genuinely unanswerable without first knowing her exact hours spent studying
items.explanation: The original decision was reasonable given the information available at the time. Updating it once better information arrived isn't evidence the first call was a mistake — it's exactly what re-triaging is supposed to do when circumstances change.
items.reference:
The claim: Triage should be revisited once real information replaces the original guesses, not fixed forever after the first pass.

Why: A changed input justifies an updated decision without implying the earlier decision was wrong given what was known then.

items.prompt: Why is re-triaging worth treating as an ongoing habit rather than a one-time step done only at the very start?
choices: Because the initial triage, by this unit's account, is always wrong and needs frequent correcting
Because even a well-reasoned initial triage is built on whatever's known at the time, and new information can change what the right call is for a specific item
Because triage should actually be redone completely from scratch every single day, regardless of new information
Because re-triaging has no real practical benefit at all, even though it does feel productive
items.explanation: The initial triage is only as good as the information behind it. As real information replaces early guesses — through direct experience, new facts, or corrections like the tax-filing deadline — specific items are worth updating, cheaply and without treating it as evidence the original process failed.
items.reference:
The claim: Triage should be revisited once real information replaces the original guesses, not fixed forever after the first pass.

Why: A changed input justifies an updated decision without implying the earlier decision was wrong given what was known then.

items.prompt: If Sofia had only 2 hours instead of 20, what does this unit predict changes about her triage?
choices: Nothing really changes — the same number of topics still get deep study, just with less time allotted each
The bar for 'deep now' rises sharply, and even the 'worth a skim' tier shrinks, since skim time is drawn from the same scarce budget
She should abandon triage as a method entirely and just study whatever comes to mind first
She should spread the two hours evenly across all nine topics, the same way Marco did with twenty
items.explanation: Heavier time pressure doesn't just compress the deep-study hours — it shrinks the entire budget, including what's left over for a quick skim. With very little time, only the single highest-priority item (or part of it) can realistically get attention; nearly everything else gets deferred to 'figure it out on arrival' rather than even a skim.
items.reference:
The claim: Heavier time pressure raises the bar for 'deep now' and shrinks the whole 'worth a skim' tier.
